sentences.text: Margaret Doyle is the person being assessed, and she is currently living in her own home with her son Kevin Doyle, who is present during the assessment. The social worker, Priya Nair, is conducting a needs assessment under the Care Act following a referral from the hospital after Margaret was dislod

The purpose of the assessment is to understand Margaret's daily living situation, identify support needs, and determine eligibility for council support, with the explicit reassurance that the goal is to support her in her current home, not to place her in a care home.

Margaret has a history of falls, including a fall on the third of March, which resulted in a fractured left wrist and required hospitalisation at St Aldhelm's for four days. She has also had two prior falls, one in the garden and one in the bathroom, which she did not report to her GP or Kevin.

Kevin Doyle, her son, is present and has been involved in her care, including shopping and helping with daily tasks. He is available to join the assessment and has expressed concern about Margaret's safety and well-being, suggesting she may be better off in a sheltered flat.

Margaret is currently unable to walk outside her home, having only gone to the end of the path and to the doctor's once, with Kevin taking her in the car. She is frightened of falling again and has not been able to walk to the shops as she did before the fall.

Margaret uses a frame indoors and a stick outdoors, but she finds the frame difficult to use due to it getting caught on rugs and doorframes. She holds on to furniture when going up and down stairs, and uses a rail on the right side when going up, but finds coming down more difficult due to the rail

Margaret is unable to bathe or shower since the fall, due to difficulty getting in and out of the bath with her injured wrist. She has not had a proper bath since January and feels unclean and embarrassed about her hair, which she cannot comb with one hand.

Getting dressed is slow and takes up to an hour, with Margaret admitting she often stays in her nightie, especially on days when she feels no need to get up. She struggles with buttons and bra hooks and has given up on tights, wearing elasticated trousers instead.

Margaret is unable to cook or use the oven or hob since the fall, citing fear of being in the kitchen and difficulty lifting pans. She eats a very limited diet, consisting of toast, soup, yoghurt, and crackers, and has lost nearly a stone since Christmas.

Margaret takes several medications, including amlodipine for blood pressure, alendronic acid for bone health, and paracetamol for wrist pain. She has missed her blood pressure tablet twice in the past week due to distraction, and she struggles with opening her dosette box due to her wrist injury.
Margaret has not had a proper meal in the past few weeks and has lost weight, with her clothes now hanging off her. She is concerned about her appetite and has not been able to cook since the fall.

Margaret has not been able to use the toilet independently due to the stairs, and she has experienced incontinence, using pads at night. She reports that she sometimes doesn't make it to the toilet in time and leaks, which causes her to wear pads.

The home environment includes a number of rugs, particularly in the hall, which are seen as trip hazards. The stairs are a significant barrier, with the bedroom and bathroom located upstairs, requiring use of a rail or frame to access.

Margaret stated that staying in her own home is the most important thing to her, saying, 'It's everything. It's my home. It's where I brought the kids up.' She also said she wants to stay in her home for as long as possible and would not move to a care home, even if it came to that.

Margaret expressed a strong desire to have a proper bath again, saying, 'I'd love to have a bath again. I'd love it.' She also said she misses being able to wash her hair and being able to go to the lunch club with her friends Joan and Pat.

Margaret said she would like to be able to cook a proper dinner again, not every day, but 'now and then. A bit of mince, some potatoes.' She also wants to see her roses, which she says are 'Frank's roses,' and to go out and look at them in the summer.

Margaret said she is lonely and feels low, especially since Frank's death in August. She said, 'I do. I'm not going to pretend I don't,' and that some days she only speaks to Biscuit and the television.

Kevin stated that he is concerned about Margaret's safety and suggested she might be better off in a sheltered flat or bungalow, saying, 'I think this house is too much for her now.' He also said he worries about her falling again.

Margaret disclosed that her grandson Jordan has been borrowing her bank card to get cash and has made withdrawals of approximately six hundred pounds over the last two months, which she did not authorise. She said she gave him the PIN when he came to help with shopping after her hospitalisation.

Margaret said she is not aware of any other financial or personal harm, and she denied any knowledge of Jordan having gambled or being in debt, stating that such claims were 'gossip' and not confirmed.

Margaret said she has not had any thoughts of harming herself or ending her life, and she said she would tell Dr Shah or Susan if her mood were to drop again. She said she has no current plans to harm herself and that she has 'too much to live for, my grandchildren, and Biscuit.'

Margaret said she is not willing to involve the police in the matter with Jordan, and she wants the issue to be resolved through direct communication with Jordan and the bank, stating, 'I don't want the police round here for Jordan. I'm not.'

The social worker has noted that there is a safeguarding concern due to the unauthorised withdrawals from Margaret's bank account, and has referred this to the safeguarding team, with the understanding that the matter will be reviewed and no police involvement will occur unless Margaret decides to,

Margaret's primary support network includes her son Kevin, who visits mainly on Sundays and sometimes midweek, and who helps with shopping and daily tasks. He is also responsible for taking her to the bank to cancel the card and get a new one.

Margaret has a daughter, Susan, who lives in Alicante, Spain, and who calls every week on Sunday nights and visits in the summer. She said Susan was very worried when Margaret had the fall and was on the phone to Kevin every day.

Brenda, who lives next door, visits most days for a minute, knocking on the wall to check in. She has been a key support figure since her husband passed and is described as a 'treasure' and 'a good neighbour'.

Margaret used to attend a lunch club at St Michael's church hall on Thursdays, which she missed after the fall. She expressed a strong desire to return and said she misses the people there, particularly Joan and Pat.

Margaret's income consists of her state pension and half of Frank's railway pension (as a widow's pension). She has approximately nine thousand pounds in savings in the Midshire building society, which includes her funeral money and money for her grandchildren.

Margaret is not currently receiving Attendance Allowance, which is a benefit for people over state pension age who need help with personal care. She said she would need help with the form, which will be completed with Kevin's assistance.

The social worker will make a referral to occupational therapy for a bath lift or bath board, a second rail on the stairs, a second frame for upstairs, and a review of the back step and pull cord light, with the OT waiting list currently around three weeks and marked as a priority due to the falls.

The social worker will make a safeguarding referral regarding the unauthorised withdrawals from Margaret's bank account, and a safeguarding team member will contact Margaret to discuss the matter, with the understanding that no police involvement will occur unless Margaret decides otherwise.
The social worker will refer Margaret for a telecare fall detection watch (the 'Careline' watch) that can detect a fall and call for help, which will be fitted within about ten days.
The social worker will write to Dr Shah at Millbrook Surgery to request a referral to the falls clinic, and to mention the weight loss, continence issues, and missed tablets.

The social worker will contact the chemist on Station Road to request a different type of dosette pack that is easier to open, as Margaret finds the current one difficult to open with her wrist injury.

The social worker will request reablement support, including morning and teatime visits to help with washing, dressing, and meals, with the request to be approved by her manager and the outcome to be communicated by the end of next week.

Kevin will take Margaret to the Midshire building society branch on Friday morning to cancel the card and get a new one with a new PIN, and will help with the Attendance Allowance and financial assessment forms.
Margaret will set her alarm clock to nine o'clock to help with her morning medication, and Kevin will show her how to use it.
The social worker will follow up with Margaret on Monday to check in on the card cancellation and to confirm the next steps, and will return to see her on Tuesday, the 15th of April at two o'clock.
If Margaret falls again and is unable to get up, the emergency number 999 should be called, and Brenda's knocking on the wall should continue as a regular check-in method.
